title: Quadragesimo Anno (1931)
hookLine: Moses is judging every case alone until his father-in-law steps in, and a pope later gives the advice a name

cards: From morning until night, the people stand around Moses, waiting for him to settle their disputes. Every case, large or small, comes to one man.
His father-in-law Jethro watches a day of it and tells him plainly, in Exodus, that this isn't good: he'll wear himself out, and the people with him.
Choose capable, honest people, Jethro says, and set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them judge the small matters, and bring the hard ones to you. Moses listens.
Much later, a pope wrote a letter that gave Jethro's kind of advice a name. Today, Quadragesimo Anno.

teach.b: First, the letter. Quadragesimo anno is Latin for in the fortieth year.
Pius the Eleventh opens by marking forty years since Leo's Rerum Novarum, looks back at what that letter set moving, and takes up questions it left open.
Second, the principle he states, which the Church now calls subsidiarity.

teach.h: DON'T TAKE WHAT THE SMALLER CAN DO.
teach.b: Pius writes that it's an injustice, and a disturbance of right order, for a larger and higher body to take over what a smaller one can do for itself. What a family can decide, the city shouldn't decide for it.
What a town can handle, a national government shouldn't swallow. Third, it cuts both ways. Subsidiarity isn't simply small is good.
Pius also says every social body exists to help its members, never to destroy or absorb them.
So when the smaller group can't manage, when a family can't build a hospital or a village can't fight a flood alone, the larger body has a duty to step in.
The Catechism puts it as support and coordination for the common good: help from above that strengthens the hands below, rather than replacing them. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday.
Subsidiarity is a form of respect.

It trusts the people closest to a problem to know something about it: the manager who lets the team decide how to reach the goal, the parent who lets a teenager plan the trip, the parish that asks the food pantry volunteers before rewriting its rules.
Moses wasn't weaker for sharing the load. Jethro's promise, in Exodus, was that the people would go home in peace.

how: Catholic teaching applies subsidiarity to families, parishes, schools and governments, and Catholics cite it in debates over which level of society should take on a task.

games.q: you're Moses, settling the people's disputes from morning until night. your father-in-law says you'll wear yourself out. what do you do?
o: keep going: only you can judge rightly.
appoint capable people over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
stop judging and let the people sort it out alone.
games.why: Moses takes Jethro's advice: small matters are judged close to home, and the hard ones come to him. sharing the load, not dropping it.

practice: Bring to mind a group where you usually make the call, at work, at home, a committee or a group chat, and find one decision the people closest to it could make without you.
Picture handing it over cleanly, offering help only if asked; if an urge comes to take it back, notice it and let it pass. If you pray, ask God for that kind of trust.

wordCard.voice: Quadragesimo Anno. In the fortieth year: Pius the Eleventh's letter after Rerum Novarum, which states the principle of subsidiarity. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: in the fortieth year. the opening words of Pius XI's letter, and so its name.

carryVoice: Your line: from the ground up. Help from above, trust in the hands below. Back tomorrow, same hill.
